q: Roughly how much of Algeria is covered by the Sahara Desert?
fact: Most Algerians live along the Mediterranean coast in the far north - the desert south is vast but almost empty.

q: Which Roman city in Algeria, founded by Emperor Trajan around 100 AD, is famous for its perfect grid of streets?
fact: Desert sand buried Timgad for about a thousand years, which is why its streets, arch and theater survive so well.

q: Algeria's national football team is nicknamed after which small desert animal?
fact: The big-eared fennec is Algeria's national animal, and the players are known as Les Fennecs.

q: Which rare antelope, found only in Angola, is the country's national symbol?
fact: It was feared extinct until camera traps caught it again in the 2000s. The football team is named after it: Palancas Negras.

q: Which partner dance and music style, now taught in studios worldwide, was born in Angola around 1980?
fact: Kizomba grew out of the older Angolan semba. Its name means 'party' in the Kimbundu language.

q: Which religion, later carried across the Atlantic to Haiti, was born in Benin and has a national holiday there?
fact: Every January 10, Benin marks Vodun Day with ceremonies, drumming and dance in the coastal town of Ouidah.

q: Ganvie in Benin is sometimes called the 'Venice of Africa'. What is it?
answer: A village on stilts in a lake
wrong: A port city crossed by canals
A town built on river barges
fact: About 20,000 people live in Ganvie on Lake Nokoue. Children learn to paddle a canoe almost as soon as they can walk.

q: The Okavango in Botswana is one of the world's largest examples of what?
fact: The Okavango River never reaches the sea. It fans out into the Kalahari and evaporates, creating a huge wildlife oasis.

q: Botswana's currency, the pula, takes its name from the Setswana word for what?
fact: In a country that is mostly Kalahari, rain is so precious that 'Pula' is also the national motto and a cheer.

q: What does the name Burkina Faso mean?
fact: The name was adopted in 1984 and combines words from two local languages. Before that the country was Upper Volta.

q: Burkina Faso's capital, Ouagadougou, hosts FESPACO, the largest African festival of what?
fact: First held in 1969 and now staged every two years, its top prize is a golden stallion named after the warrior princess Yennenga.

q: Burundi is famous for a UNESCO-listed performance tradition built around which instrument?
fact: The drummers enter with heavy drums balanced on their heads, then leap and spin while they play.

q: Bujumbura, Burundi's largest city, lies on the shore of which lake?
fact: Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake in the world, stretching about 670 km from Burundi to Zambia.

q: Which singer from Cabo Verde, known as the 'Barefoot Diva', made the island music style morna famous worldwide?
fact: She performed without shoes all her life. The airport on her home island of Sao Vicente is named after her.

q: How many main islands make up Cabo Verde?
fact: Nine of the ten are inhabited. The islands had no people at all until Portuguese sailors arrived in the 1400s.

q: In 1990, Cameroon became the first African team to reach which stage of the men's football World Cup?
fact: Roger Milla, aged 38, scored four goals and celebrated each one with a dance at the corner flag.

q: Cameroon's name comes from a Portuguese word for which animal, once found in huge numbers in a local river?
fact: Explorers in 1472 named the Wouri estuary Rio dos Camaroes, the River of Prawns.

q: A forest clearing called Dzanga Bai in the Central African Republic is famous for daily gatherings of which animals?
fact: Up to 150 elephants at a time come to drink its mineral-rich water. It is nicknamed the village of elephants.

q: Besides French, which African language is official in the Central African Republic?
fact: Sango began as a trade language along the Ubangi River and is now understood by almost everyone in the country.

q: What is unusual about Chad's flag of blue, yellow and red vertical stripes?
wrong: It is the world's oldest flag
It is taller than it is wide
It has a different back side
fact: Only the shade of blue differs slightly. Chad adopted its flag in 1959, when Romania's still carried a coat of arms.

q: A 7-million-year-old skull nicknamed 'Toumai', found in Chad in 2001, may belong to one of the oldest known what?
fact: Toumai means 'hope of life' in the local Daza language. The find suggests that early human relatives lived far beyond East Africa.

q: Which 'living fossil' fish, believed extinct for 65 million years until 1938, lives in deep water off Comoros?
fact: Comorian fishermen had long known it as gombessa. It can grow to two meters and may live for close to a century.

q: Comoros is a leading producer of ylang-ylang flower oil. What is the oil mainly used for?
fact: The sweet essence goes into many famous perfumes, and the country is nicknamed the Perfume Islands.

q: Congo's capital, Brazzaville, faces which other capital city directly across a river?
fact: Apart from Rome and Vatican City, Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the closest pair of capitals in the world.

q: The 'Sapeurs' of Brazzaville in Congo are famous for what?
fact: La Sape is a movement of ordinary working men who dress as dandies in bright tailored suits and treat style as an art.

q: Which shy relative of the giraffe, with zebra-striped legs, lives in the wild only in DR Congo?
fact: The okapi was unknown to Western science until 1901. It appears on the country's banknotes.

q: From 1971 to 1997, DR Congo was known by which name?
fact: Zaire came from a local phrase meaning 'the river that swallows all rivers' - the Congo.

q: DR Congo mines well over half of the world's supply of which metal used in phone and car batteries?
fact: Cobalt helps keep rechargeable batteries stable. Most of it comes from the copper belt in the country's southeast.

q: Lake Assal in Djibouti holds which African record?
fact: Its shore lies 155 m below sea level, and its water is about ten times saltier than the ocean.

q: Djibouti sits on the Bab-el-Mandeb, a strait linking the Red Sea with which body of water?
fact: The strait's name means Gate of Tears in Arabic. Ships sailing between Europe and Asia by way of Suez all pass through it.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still stands in Egypt today?
fact: It is the oldest of the seven and the only one to survive. For almost 4,000 years it was the tallest structure on Earth.

q: Egypt's Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea with which other sea?
fact: Opened in 1869, it lets ships sail between Europe and Asia without going all the way around Africa.

q: The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, was the key to reading what?
fact: It carries the same decree in three scripts, one of them Greek, which let Champollion crack the code in 1822.

q: About how old was Egypt's Great Pyramid already when Cleopatra was born?
fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the pyramid.

q: Koshari, a street-food favorite often called Egypt's national dish, mixes rice and pasta with what?
fact: It is topped with spicy tomato sauce, chickpeas and crispy fried onions - and contains no meat at all.

q: Equatorial Guinea is the only country in Africa where which language is official?
fact: It was a Spanish colony until 1968. French and Portuguese are official there too.

q: What is surprising about Equatorial Guinea and the equator?
answer: The equator misses all of its land
wrong: The equator is its southern border
The equator cuts it in two halves
fact: The mainland and Bioko island lie just north of the line, and the small island of Annobon lies just south of it.

q: Eritrea's capital, Asmara, became a UNESCO site for its 1930s buildings in which style?
fact: Its landmarks include a gas station shaped like an airplane, with concrete wings stretching 15 meters to each side.

q: The name Eritrea comes from the ancient Greek name for what?
fact: The Greeks called it the Erythraean Sea, from 'erythros', meaning red. Eritrea has over 1,000 km of Red Sea coast.

q: Until 2018, Eswatini was known by which name?
fact: The king announced the change at a celebration of 50 years of independence. Eswatini means 'land of the Swazis'.

q: The Umhlanga, a famous yearly ceremony in Eswatini, is also known by which name?
fact: Tens of thousands of young women cut tall reeds, present them to the Queen Mother and dance in traditional dress.

q: How many months are there in Ethiopia's traditional calendar?
fact: Twelve months have 30 days each and a short thirteenth has five or six. The calendar also runs seven to eight years behind the Western one.

q: According to legend, an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi discovered which drink after his goats began to dance?
fact: Coffee still grows wild in Ethiopia's highland forests, and a traditional coffee ceremony can last over an hour.

q: The town of Lalibela in Ethiopia is famous for 11 medieval churches made in what way?
fact: Workers cut them from the top down about 800 years ago. The most famous, St George, is shaped like a cross.

q: Injera, Ethiopia's spongy sourdough flatbread, is traditionally made from which tiny grain?
fact: Injera is plate, cutlery and food at once: stews are served on top of it and scooped up with torn-off pieces.

q: How did Ethiopia's Abebe Bikila famously run when he won the Olympic marathon in Rome in 1960?
fact: He was the first Black African to win Olympic gold, and he won again in Tokyo four years later - this time in shoes.

q: Roughly how much of Gabon is covered by rainforest?
fact: In 2002 Gabon set aside more than a tenth of its land as 13 national parks, all created on the same day.

q: At Oklo in Gabon, scientists found the only known natural example of what?
fact: About two billion years ago, rich uranium deposits there kept chain reactions going on their own for hundreds of thousands of years.

q: Gambia's long, narrow shape follows the course of what?
fact: The country is a strip of land never more than about 50 km wide, running along both banks of the Gambia River.

q: For decades, how did voters in Gambia cast their ballots?
wrong: By tying knots in a rope
fact: Each candidate has a painted drum. A bell inside rings when a marble drops, so nobody can vote twice.

q: Which brightly patterned woven cloth, once reserved for Ashanti royalty, comes from Ghana?
fact: Kente is woven in narrow strips that are sewn together, and each pattern and color carries its own meaning.

q: Lake Volta in Ghana holds which world record?
fact: Created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965, it covers about 8,500 square km - more than 3% of Ghana.

q: In Ghana's Akan tradition, names like Kofi and Kwame tell you what about a person?
fact: Kofi is a boy born on a Friday and Kwame on a Saturday. Former UN chief Kofi Annan was indeed born on a Friday.

q: Guinea is called the 'water tower of West Africa'. Why?
wrong: It rains there every single day
A huge lake fills its center
fact: The Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers all start in Guinea's highlands before flowing through a string of other countries.

q: Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the main ore of which metal?
fact: Bauxite is a reddish rock. It takes about four tons of it to make one ton of aluminum.

q: The Bijagos islands of Guinea-Bissau are known for which unusual animals living in salty coastal water?
fact: The hippos of Orango island wade through mangroves and swim in the sea between islands.

q: Why does Guinea-Bissau have 'Bissau' in its name?
answer: It is the name of its capital
wrong: It is the name of its main river
fact: The capital was added to the name at independence to avoid confusion with the neighboring country of Guinea.

q: A huge basilica in Yamoussoukro, Ivory Coast, completed in 1989, was modeled on which famous building?
fact: Guinness lists it as the largest church in the world. Counting the cross on its dome, it stands even taller than the one it copies.

q: What is the nickname of Ivory Coast's national football team?
fact: The country is named for the ivory once traded on its coast, and an elephant also appears on its coat of arms.

q: Each year over a million wildebeest cross into Kenya's Maasai Mara from which famous neighboring park?
fact: The Great Migration follows the rains in a loop. The dramatic Mara River crossings peak from July to September.

q: In a specially staged run in Vienna in 2019, Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to do what?
answer: Run a marathon in under 2 hours
fact: His 1:59:40 used rotating pacemakers, so it was not an official record. Kenya's Sabastian Sawe ran the first official sub-2 marathon, 1:59:30, in London in 2026.

q: Kenya's Wangari Maathai won the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize after founding a movement that did what?
fact: Her Green Belt Movement has planted tens of millions of trees. She was the first African woman to win the Peace Prize.

q: M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007, made it easy to do what with a basic mobile phone?
fact: It let millions of people without bank accounts pay and save by text message, years before smartphone wallets.

q: Lesotho holds which geographic world record?
answer: Highest low point of any country
fact: Even its lowest spot is 1,400 m above sea level. It is the only country lying entirely above 1,000 m.

q: Which sport, rare in Africa, can be practiced at a resort in Lesotho's Maloti Mountains?
fact: Afriski sits about 3,000 m up and opens its slope in the southern winter, from June to August.

q: Liberia's capital, Monrovia, is named after whom?
fact: Liberia was founded in the 1800s by freed people from the United States, and President James Monroe backed the project.

q: Liberia's George Weah, later elected president, is the only African footballer to have won which award?
fact: He won it in 1995 while playing for AC Milan, and became president of Liberia in 2018.

q: Liberia's flag closely resembles the flag of the United States. How many stars does it have?
fact: The single star gives Liberia its nickname, the Lone Star. The flag's 11 stripes stand for the signers of its independence.

q: From 1977 to 2011, what was unique about Libya's national flag?
answer: It was plain green, with no design
wrong: It showed a map of the country
It had a different back side
fact: It was the only national flag in the world with a single color and nothing else on it.

q: Libya's Great Man-Made River is a huge network of pipes. What does it carry?
fact: It pumps ancient 'fossil' water from deep desert aquifers through thousands of kilometers of pipe to the coastal cities.

q: Which group of animals is native only to Madagascar?
fact: There are about 100 kinds of lemur, from the tiny mouse lemur to the indri, which sings like a whale.

q: Madagascar is the world's leading producer of which spice?
fact: Each vanilla orchid flower must be pollinated by hand, which is why vanilla is the second most expensive spice after saffron.

q: A famous 'Avenue' near Morondava in Madagascar is lined with which giant trees?
fact: Six of the world's eight baobab species grow only in Madagascar. Their fat trunks store water for the dry season.

q: Madagascar's Malagasy language is most closely related to languages spoken where?
fact: The first settlers sailed about 6,000 km across the Indian Ocean from Southeast Asia more than a thousand years ago.

q: Lake Malawi is home to more species of what than any other lake on Earth?
fact: It holds up to 1,000 species of colorful cichlids, most found nowhere else - a favorite of aquarium keepers.

q: As a teenager in Malawi in 2002, William Kamkwamba became famous for building what from scrap?
fact: Using a library book, bicycle parts and blue gum poles, he brought electricity to his family home. His story became a film.

q: Mansa Musa, who ruled the Mali Empire in the 1300s, is often described as what?
fact: On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 he gave away so much gold in Cairo that its price fell for years.

q: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the world's largest building made of what?
fact: Every year the whole town turns out for a festival to re-plaster its walls with fresh mud by hand.

q: The Richat Structure in Mauritania, a ring of rock 40 km wide that astronauts use as a landmark, has which nickname?
fact: From orbit it looks like a giant bullseye. It is not a crater, but a dome of rock worn down by erosion.

q: Mauritania's iron-ore railway is famous for running some of the world's what?
fact: A single train can stretch 2.5 km, with over 200 wagons crossing about 700 km of the Sahara to the coast.

q: Which famous flightless bird lived only on Mauritius before dying out in the 1600s?
fact: With no predators on the island, the dodo had no fear of people. It vanished within a century of sailors arriving.

q: Mauritius is the only country in Africa where which religion has the most followers?
fact: About half of Mauritians are Hindu, descendants of workers who came from India to the sugar plantations in the 1800s.

q: The university often called the oldest still operating in the world, founded in 859, is in which Moroccan city?
fact: By tradition, al-Qarawiyyin was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, who spent her inheritance on a mosque and school.

q: The Moroccan mountain town of Chefchaouen is famous for buildings painted which color?
fact: Nearly every wall, door and staircase in its old town is washed in shades of blue. Marrakesh, by contrast, is the Red City.

q: The Moroccan dish tagine is named after what?
answer: The clay pot it is cooked in
wrong: The city where it was invented
The spice blend that flavors it
fact: The pot's cone-shaped lid traps steam and returns it to the stew, so it needs very little water.

q: At the 2022 World Cup, Morocco became the first African team ever to reach which stage?
fact: The Atlas Lions beat Belgium, Spain and Portugal along the way, and finished fourth.

q: Which unusual object appears on Mozambique's flag, crossed with a hoe on top of an open book?
fact: It is an AK-47, the only modern assault rifle on any national flag. It stands for defense, the book for education and the hoe for farming.

q: Which fiery chili sauce, famous on grilled chicken, is closely tied to Mozambique and its Portuguese past?
fact: Piri-piri means 'pepper pepper' in Swahili. Portuguese traders brought the chilies from the Americas centuries ago.

q: The Namib, which gives Namibia its name, is thought to be the world's oldest what?
fact: It has been dry for at least 55 million years, and its red dunes at Sossusvlei are among the tallest on Earth.

q: Namibia's foggy Skeleton Coast is littered with whale bones and the remains of what else?
fact: Thick fog and strong currents have wrecked more than a thousand ships there. Sailors once called it the Gates of Hell.

q: The Hoba, a 60-ton block lying on a farm in Namibia, is the largest known what on Earth?
fact: It landed about 80,000 years ago and has never been moved. Oddly, it left no crater.

q: Until 1973, the Tree of Tenere in Niger was famous for being what?
answer: The most isolated tree on Earth
fact: No other tree stood within 400 km. It was knocked down by a truck, and a metal sculpture now marks the spot.

q: Niger has long been one of the world's main sources of which metal used as fuel in nuclear power plants?
fact: The mines lie near the desert town of Arlit, on the edge of the Air Mountains in the Sahara.

q: Nigeria's film industry, one of the world's largest by number of movies made, goes by which nickname?
fact: It turns out well over a thousand films a year, many of them shot in just a few weeks.

q: In 1986, Nigerian writer Wole Soyinka won which international prize, a first for sub-Saharan Africa?
fact: Soyinka made his name as a playwright and poet. South Africa's Albert Luthuli had won the Peace Prize back in 1960.

q: Nigeria and Ghana have a famous friendly rivalry over who cooks the best version of which dish?
fact: Jollof is rice simmered in a spicy tomato sauce. It probably began in Senegal, home of the old Jolof kingdom.

q: Which music style did Nigeria's Fela Kuti create in the 1970s by mixing funk and jazz with West African rhythms?
fact: His songs could run for half an hour. Today's Afrobeats pop, with an added 's', takes its name from his sound.

q: Rwanda is known by which nickname?
fact: Almost the whole country is hilly and lies more than 1,000 m above sea level.

q: Rwanda's parliament holds the world record for the highest share of what?
fact: More than 60% of the seats in its lower house are held by women - the highest proportion of any country.

q: For a few years in the early 1900s, tiny Sao Tome and Principe was the world's largest producer of what?
fact: The islands are still nicknamed the Chocolate Islands, and old plantation estates called rocas dot the hills.

q: A monument on Rolas, a small islet of Sao Tome and Principe, marks which line?
fact: Visitors can stand with one foot in each hemisphere. The line crosses the islet just south of the main island.

q: Lake Retba in Senegal is famous for water of which color?
fact: Salt-loving algae give the lake its color, and workers wade in to dig salt from its bottom by hand.

q: The famous rally that used to finish in Senegal's capital, Dakar, traditionally started in which city?
fact: The Paris-Dakar crossed the Sahara from 1979. The race later moved to South America and Saudi Arabia but kept the name.

q: Senegal's football team is called the Lions of Teranga. What does the Wolof word 'teranga' mean?
fact: Teranga is the national value of welcoming guests generously. Sharing a meal from one big bowl is part of it.

q: The coco de mer palm of Seychelles produces the world's largest what?
fact: A single seed can weigh over 15 kg and takes six or seven years to ripen. The palm grows wild on just two islands.

q: Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles is home to the world's largest population of which animal?
fact: Well over 100,000 giant tortoises live there - several times more than on the Galapagos Islands.

q: The name Sierra Leone, given by a Portuguese explorer in 1462, means what?
fact: Pedro de Sintra may have been thinking of the shape of the hills, or of thunder rolling around them like a roar.

q: Why is the capital of Sierra Leone called Freetown?
answer: It was founded for freed slaves
wrong: Its land was given away free
It never had a city wall
fact: The settlement was founded in 1792 by people freed from slavery, many of them arriving by ship from Nova Scotia.

q: Somalia holds which record among the countries of mainland Africa?
fact: Its coast runs for more than 3,000 km along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

q: Somalia is one of the world's main sources of which fragrant tree resin, traded since ancient times?
fact: The resin is tapped from Boswellia trees and has been burned as incense for more than 5,000 years.

q: How many capital cities does South Africa have?
fact: Pretoria houses the government, Cape Town the parliament and Bloemfontein the top appeals court.

q: In 1967, a surgeon in Cape Town, South Africa, performed the world's first what?
fact: Dr Christiaan Barnard led the operation at Groote Schuur Hospital, and it made headlines around the world.

q: Which cape in South Africa is the true southernmost point of Africa?
fact: It lies about 150 km southeast of the more famous Cape of Good Hope and officially divides the Atlantic and Indian oceans.

q: South Africa's Springboks have won a record four World Cups in which sport?
fact: They lifted the trophy in 1995, 2007, 2019 and 2023. Nelson Mandela handed over the first one, wearing the team jersey.

q: Which unexpected birds live on Boulders Beach near Cape Town, South Africa?
fact: African penguins settled on the beach in the 1980s. They are also called jackass penguins for their donkey-like bray.

q: Which caffeine-free 'red bush' tea grows naturally only in South Africa's Cederberg mountains?
fact: Rooibos is not a true tea but a shrub. Its green needles turn red-brown as they are left to ferment in the sun.

q: South Sudan became independent in 2011. Which title has it held ever since?
fact: It became the 193rd member of the United Nations after a vote in which almost 99% chose independence.

q: The Sudd in South Sudan, fed by the White Nile, is one of the world's largest what?
fact: In the rainy season the swamp can swell to roughly the size of England. Its name comes from the Arabic for 'barrier'.

q: Sudan has more of which ancient monuments than Egypt does?
fact: The kings and queens of Kush built over 200 of them, smaller and steeper than Egypt's, at sites such as Meroe.

q: Which two rivers meet at Khartoum, the capital of Sudan?
fact: For a stretch the two flow side by side in different colors before mixing into the single Nile.

q: Tanzania's Mount Kilimanjaro is the world's tallest example of what?
fact: It rises alone from the plains to 5,895 m, with no mountain range around it, and is capped by shrinking glaciers.

q: The name Tanzania was created in 1964 by blending the names of which two places?
fact: The mainland of Tanganyika and the islands of Zanzibar united that year to form a single country.

q: Which rock star was born in 1946 on the island of Zanzibar, now part of Tanzania?
fact: The Queen singer was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, where his childhood home is now a museum.

q: Which blue-violet gemstone is mined in only one place on Earth, near Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania?
fact: Discovered in 1967, it was named by the jeweler Tiffany & Co. to honor the country.

q: What is unusual about the location of Lome, the capital of Togo?
answer: It sits right on a national border
wrong: It sits on an island in a lake
It sits in an old volcano crater
It sits high on a mountain ridge
fact: The city's western edge is the border with Ghana. You can walk from downtown Lome into another country.

q: Which striker, African Footballer of the Year in 2008, is the all-time top scorer for Togo?
fact: He scored 32 goals for Togo and led the team to its first World Cup in 2006. His clubs included Arsenal and Real Madrid.

q: Which ancient city, the great rival of Rome and home of Hannibal, stood on the coast of what is now Tunisia?
fact: Its ruins lie in a seaside suburb of Tunis. Its general Hannibal famously led war elephants across the Alps.

q: Which film series shot its desert planet Tatooine in Tunisia and borrowed the name from a local town?
fact: The real town is Tataouine. Luke Skywalker's home was filmed in an underground hotel in Matmata that still takes guests.

q: Which hot chili paste, a staple of Tunisian cooking, was added to UNESCO's cultural heritage list in 2022?
fact: It is made from sun-dried peppers, garlic, caraway and olive oil, and is eaten with almost everything.

q: At Jinja in Uganda, which great river begins its journey out of Lake Victoria?
fact: From here the water of the White Nile takes about three months to reach the Mediterranean Sea.

q: Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable Forest shelters roughly half of the world's remaining what?
fact: Only about a thousand mountain gorillas exist. Visitors trek for hours to spend a single hour with one family.

q: In Uganda, a 'rolex' is a popular street food. What is it?
answer: An omelet rolled in a flatbread
wrong: A skewer of grilled goat meat
fact: The name is a play on 'rolled eggs'. It is cooked on a hot plate at roadside stalls and wrapped in a chapati.

q: Which bird stands at the center of Uganda's flag?
fact: The crane is known for its gentle nature and golden crown of feathers. The national football team is nicknamed the Cranes.

q: In Zambia, Victoria Falls is known as Mosi-oa-Tunya. What does the name mean?
fact: Its spray rises hundreds of meters and can be seen from 30 km away.

q: What unusual thing happened to Zambia's team during the 1964 Tokyo Olympics?
wrong: It won gold in its very first event
It marched in without any flag
It arrived after the Games ended
fact: The athletes arrived as Northern Rhodesia. Independence came on the day of the closing ceremony, and they left as Zambia.

q: The name Zimbabwe comes from a Shona phrase meaning what?
fact: It refers to Great Zimbabwe, a medieval city whose granite walls, up to 11 m high, were built without mortar.

q: In 2009, Zimbabwe issued its largest-ever banknote. What was its face value?
fact: The note was withdrawn within months. Today it is a popular collector's item around the world.

q: The bird on Zimbabwe's flag is based on what?
fact: Eight soapstone birds once stood on pillars at Great Zimbabwe. They may show a bateleur eagle or a fish eagle.

q: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
fact: Algeria has held the title since 2011, when Sudan split in two. It is the tenth-largest country in the world.

q: Which is the most populous country in Africa?
fact: With well over 200 million people, Nigeria is home to about one in six Africans.

q: Which is the smallest country on the African mainland by area?
fact: At its widest it is under 50 km across, and it is surrounded by Senegal on every side except its short coast.

q: Which is the smallest country in Africa, by both area and population?
fact: Seychelles has only about 120,000 people, spread over 115 islands in the Indian Ocean.

q: Which country grows about 40% of the world's cocoa, more than any other?
fact: Ivory Coast harvests around two million tons of cocoa beans a year, most of them grown on small family farms.

q: Which country contains the westernmost point of mainland Africa?
fact: The Pointe des Almadies lies on the Cap-Vert peninsula in Dakar - the 'green cape' that the islands of Cabo Verde are named after.

q: The legendary desert city of Timbuktu is in which country?
fact: Once a rich center of trade and learning, it is famous for hundreds of thousands of centuries-old manuscripts.

q: The famous Benin Bronzes were made in a kingdom located in which present-day country?
fact: The Kingdom of Benin was centered on Benin City in southern Nigeria. The modern country of Benin only took its name in 1975.

q: Which country hosted the first football World Cup held in Africa, in 2010?
fact: The tournament is remembered for the buzzing vuvuzela horns in the stands. Spain won its first title.

q: Which country has won football's Africa Cup of Nations a record seven times?
fact: Egypt won the very first tournament in 1957, and three in a row between 2006 and 2010.

q: Which country contains the northernmost point of Africa?
fact: The spot is Cape Angela, a rocky headland near the port city of Bizerte, on the Mediterranean.

q: Which country is home to the largest elephant population in Africa?
fact: About 130,000 elephants roam Botswana - roughly a third of all the savanna elephants left in Africa.

q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
fact: Lesotho is one of only three countries in the world enclosed by a single neighbor, with San Marino and Vatican City.

q: Lake Victoria is shared by Tanzania, Uganda and which third country?
fact: Kenya has only about 6% of the lake, including the port city of Kisumu.

q: Which country's flag features a Maasai shield and two crossed spears?
fact: The shield and spears stand for the defense of freedom. Black, red and green stripes run behind them.

q: Which country's red flag carries a green five-pointed star known as the Seal of Solomon?
fact: The star was added in 1915 to set the plain red flag apart from other red banners.

q: Which country's green, yellow and red flag inspired the colors of many other African flags?
fact: As Africa's oldest independent state, Ethiopia became a symbol for nations winning their freedom in the 1950s and 60s.

q: Which country was long known to outsiders as Abyssinia?
fact: The name was used in Europe for centuries. Its emperors traced their line back to King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

q: The small highland town of Iten, known as the 'Home of Champions' for its distance runners, is in which country?
fact: Iten sits 2,400 m up on the edge of the Rift Valley, and runners from all over the world train there.

q: Which country is nicknamed the 'Rainbow Nation'?
fact: Archbishop Desmond Tutu coined the phrase in 1994 to describe the country's many peoples and cultures.

q: Africa's oldest national park, Virunga, founded in 1925, is in which country?
fact: Virunga packs volcanoes, glaciers, savanna and rainforest into one park, and shelters mountain gorillas.

q: People from which country are called Malagasy?
fact: Malagasy is also the name of the national language, spoken across the whole island.

q: Which is the only African country with coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea?
fact: At the Strait of Gibraltar, Morocco lies just 14 km from Spain.

q: Which country borders nine others, more than any other in Africa?
fact: Despite its huge size and long list of neighbors, DR Congo has only about 40 km of coastline.

q: Which country was known as South West Africa until 1990?
fact: It was a German colony and was then ruled by South Africa. German street names and bakeries survive to this day.

q: Which country's national football team is nicknamed the Black Stars?
fact: The name comes from the black star at the center of Ghana's flag, a symbol of African freedom.

q: Which country banned plastic bags in 2008 and holds a monthly community clean-up day?
fact: On the last Saturday of each month, Rwandans join in Umuganda, a morning of shared neighborhood work.

q: Victoria Falls lies on the border between Zambia and which other country?
fact: The falls are on the Zambezi River and are about 1,700 m wide - one of the largest curtains of falling water on Earth.

q: Which country has the largest proven oil reserves in Africa?
fact: Libya's reserves are estimated at about 48 billion barrels, ahead of Nigeria's.

q: The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert. Roughly how big is it?
answer: About the size of the USA
wrong: About twice the size of Russia
fact: It covers about 9 million square km of North Africa. Most of it is bare rock and gravel, not sand dunes.

q: Which river flows north for more than 6,600 km before emptying into the Mediterranean Sea?
fact: Ancient Egypt depended on its yearly flood, which left a strip of rich black soil along the banks.

q: Which African river is the deepest river in the world, with spots more than 220 m deep?
fact: It is second only to the Amazon in the amount of water it carries, and it crosses the equator twice.

q: Mount Kilimanjaro has three volcanic cones. Which one is the highest?
fact: Uhuru Peak on Kibo's crater rim is the highest point in Africa at 5,895 m. Uhuru means freedom in Swahili.

q: Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake. It is also the world's largest what?
fact: It covers almost 70,000 square km, about the size of the Republic of Ireland, yet its average depth is only around 40 m.

q: What is East Africa's Great Rift Valley slowly doing to the continent?
fact: The plates pull apart by a few millimeters a year. In millions of years a new ocean may cut East Africa off from the rest.

q: Which language, rich in Arabic loanwords, is the most widely spoken in East Africa?
fact: Well over 100 million people speak it, mostly as a second language. 'Safari' and 'hakuna matata' are both Swahili.

q: How many countries in Africa are members of the United Nations?
fact: That is more than any other continent - over a quarter of all UN member states.

q: The 'Big Five' of an African safari are the lion, leopard, elephant, buffalo and which other animal?
fact: The term comes from old hunting days: these were the five animals most dangerous to track on foot.

q: Africa is the only continent crossed by both the equator and which other line?
fact: The two lines meet in the Atlantic Ocean in the Gulf of Guinea, at a point jokingly called Null Island.

q: Which stretchy dough, pounded from cassava, yams or plantains, is a staple food across West and Central Africa?
fact: It is eaten with the fingers: pinch off a piece, dent it with your thumb and use it to scoop up soup.

q: The djembe, now played all over the world, is a West African type of what?
fact: It is carved from a single piece of hardwood, topped with goatskin and played with bare hands.

q: The CFA franc is a currency shared by how many African countries?
fact: It comes in a West African and a Central African version, each used by a group of mostly French-speaking countries.

q: Which desert covers most of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa?
fact: It is not a true desert everywhere: parts get enough rain for grass, trees and huge herds of antelope.
